sections.title: About right

lines: From vCenter's own statistics of the last 30 days (2-hour averages) - the hypervisor's measurements, nothing from inside the guests - and each VM's busiest days of the last year (daily averages).
CPU: the busiest 5% of the time is left out (the 95th percentile); vCPUs are suggested so that use would be about 70%, never more than 50% fewer at once, at least 2 (Windows 2).

More vCPUs or memory only from the last 30 days: 85% CPU (90% active memory) or more at the 95th percentile, and on 3 separate days or more (a day counts when its busiest 2-hour average got there). Fewer days: watch.

The year's busiest day never adds: it only holds a cut back, and the reason says how many days of the year were within 10 points of it (a one-off, or a pattern such as month end). A day above 100% is left out as suspect. A day's average is a percent of the vCPUs (or memory) the VM had that day: vCPUs added since make it read high, which only holds a cut back; vCPUs removed since make it read low.

Confidence: High with no doubt, Medium with one, Low with two or more. A doubt: fewer than 21 days of history, a suspect day left out, the busiest day holding the cut back, the 95th percentile within 10 points of the line it crossed (for growth: busy on fewer than half the days), or less memory for a VM of 32 GB or more with 10% or less active (check the application's own memory setting first).
CPU ready is the time a VM waited for a physical CPU: 5% or more is said. It often means too many vCPUs, or a busy host.

Memory (the less certain one): vCenter sees the memory a guest touched in the last minutes (active memory), not what it needs - file caches and databases want more. So the suggestion is its active memory plus 100%, never more than 50% less at once, at least 2 GB (Windows 4), and only when it is 25% and 2 GB smaller or more.
Suggestions only: nothing was changed. Check a VM's own peaks (month end, patching, backups) before resizing it; removing vCPUs or memory needs the VM shut down.
